stimuli.title: The Lamp at Gull Point
stimuli.text:
The storm arrived an hour before dark, flinging rain against the cottage windows like handfuls of gravel. Mara pressed her nose to the glass and watched the sea heave itself up the rocks below Gull Point.

"Grandad, shouldn't we light the lamp?" she asked.

Her grandfather did not answer. He was asleep in his armchair, his bad leg propped on a stool, the newspaper slipping from his fingers. The doctor had told him to rest for a fortnight, and for once he had listened.

Mara looked at the brass key hanging by the door. She had climbed the lighthouse stairs a hundred times, but always behind Grandad, always carrying the tea flask while he carried the key. She knew every step of the routine: trim the wick, polish the glass, strike the match, wind the clockwork that turned the great lens.

Somewhere out in the grey, a ship's horn moaned.

Mara took the key.

The wind tore at her coat as she crossed the yard, and the iron door of the tower groaned on its hinges. Inside, the stairs spiralled up into darkness. She counted them under her breath, the way Grandad did: one hundred and twelve. By the top her legs were shaking, but her hands were steady as she struck the match.

The flame caught. Mara wound the handle until the clockwork clicked, and slowly, solemnly, the beam began to sweep across the water.

When she came back down, soaked to the skin, Grandad was standing in the cottage doorway, leaning on his stick. He did not scold her. He simply looked up at the turning light, then at Mara, and nodded once, the way he nodded at the end of a job well done.

stimuli.title: Help for Hedgehogs
stimuli.text:
Hedgehogs were once a common sight in British gardens, but their numbers have fallen sharply in recent decades. Wildlife groups believe there are several reasons. Hedges have been removed to make bigger fields, roads cut across the places where hedgehogs feed, and many gardens are now surrounded by solid fences or walls.

That last problem matters more than you might think. A hedgehog may travel a mile or more in a single night, snuffling for beetles, caterpillars and worms. If every garden is sealed off, it cannot reach enough food or find a mate.

The good news is that one of the simplest ways to help costs almost nothing. Many people now cut a small hole, about 13 centimetres square, at the bottom of their fence. This is big enough for a hedgehog but too small for most pets. When neighbours do the same, a chain of gardens becomes a "hedgehog highway".

There are other ways to help, too. Leaving a corner of the garden a little wild, with a pile of logs or leaves, gives hedgehogs somewhere to shelter and to hibernate through the winter, usually from about November until March. A shallow dish of fresh water is welcome in dry weather. However, you should never put out bread or milk: milk can make hedgehogs very ill. If you want to offer food, meaty cat or dog food is far safer.

Finally, check before you strim long grass or light a bonfire, as a hedgehog may be sleeping inside. A few careful minutes could save a life.

stimuli.title: The Pumpkin Plan
stimuli.text:
Every year, Grandad Ray entered the giant pumpkin contest at the village show, and every year he came second to Mrs Okafor, whose pumpkins were rumoured to be fed on a secret mixture she would not share with anyone.

"This is our year, Sami," Grandad said in April, pressing a single seed into a pot of compost on the allotment shed's windowsill. "I can feel it in my bones."

Sami had heard this before. Still, he visited the allotment every day after school that summer. He watered the pumpkin when the soil was dry, chased away slugs with a torch on warm evenings, and laid straw under the swelling fruit so it would not rot on the damp ground. By August it was the size of a wheelbarrow, its skin glowing orange like a sunset.

On the morning of the show, it took four people and a borrowed trolley to move it. The judges weighed it twice. Then they weighed Mrs Okafor's.

"Second place," announced the judge, "by just two kilograms."

Grandad Ray was quiet on the walk home. Sami could not think of anything helpful to say, so he said nothing at all.

At the allotment gate, Mrs Okafor was waiting. She held out a folded scrap of paper.

"You've earned this," she said, "and so has your grandson. I watched him out here with that torch every evening." She smiled. "There is no secret mixture, you know. Just patience."

Grandad unfolded the paper and laughed so loudly that a pigeon took off from the shed roof. Written on it, in neat capitals, was a single word: WATER.

stimuli.title: When the Thames Froze
stimuli.text:
Today it is hard to imagine, but there were winters long ago when the River Thames in London froze so solidly that people held fairs on the ice. These events became known as frost fairs.

The freezing was helped by the old London Bridge. It stood on many thick stone supports with narrow arches between them, which slowed the river down above the bridge. The slow water froze far more easily than a fast-flowing river would. The winters of that period were also often colder than winters in Britain are now.

When the ice was thick enough, Londoners turned the river into a street. Traders put up tents and stalls selling hot food, gingerbread and drinks. There were games of skittles, puppet shows and even printing presses, where visitors could buy a card printed with their own name and the words "printed on the Thames".

The fairs were great fun, but they were also dangerous. The ice could crack without warning, and people sometimes fell through into the freezing water below.

The last frost fair was held in 1814. Some years later the old bridge was pulled down and replaced by a new bridge with wider arches. Later in the nineteenth century, embankments were built along the river's banks, making it narrower and faster. Combined with milder winters, these changes mean that the Thames in central London is now very unlikely ever to freeze over again.

stimuli.title: The Night Train
stimuli.text:
The night train hums along the line,
a lantern-snake of gold,
it threads the sleeping villages
and hurries through the cold.

The cows lie dreaming in the fields,
the owls look up and stare;
it whispers past the silent church
and leaves a ribbon on the air.

Inside, a girl with tired eyes
counts stations on her hand:
four more, three more, two more, one,
and then her own home land.

Her grandma waits beneath the clock,
her scarf pulled to her chin.
The night train sighs, the doors slide back,
and warmth comes rushing in.

stimuli.title: Mary Anning, Fossil Hunter
stimuli.text:
Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small town on the Dorset coast. The crumbling cliffs there are packed with fossils, the stony remains of creatures that lived millions of years ago. Mary's family was poor, and as a child she helped them earn money by collecting fossils from the beach and selling them to visitors.

When Mary was about twelve, she and her brother Joseph uncovered the skeleton of an ichthyosaur, a sea reptile with a long, toothed snout. It was one of the first ever found. Over the following years Mary made many more important discoveries, including the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a reptile with a small head and a very long neck.

Fossil hunting was risky work. The best finds appeared after storms, when fresh rock fell from the cliffs, and landslides were a constant danger. Mary once narrowly escaped a landslide that killed her dog, Tray.

Although scientists across Britain studied her finds, Mary did not always receive the credit she deserved. As a woman, she was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London, and some of her discoveries were described by men who did not mention her name.

Mary Anning died in 1847. Today she is celebrated as one of the most important fossil hunters in history, and her work helped people to understand that some kinds of animals had lived long ago and then died out completely.

questions.stem: Why was Mara's grandfather not able to light the lamp himself?
options: He had lost the key to the lighthouse.
He was out in the storm looking for a ship.
He was asleep, resting his bad leg as the doctor had told him.
He did not know how to work the clockwork.
questions.explanation: The passage says he was asleep in his armchair, his bad leg propped on a stool, because "the doctor had told him to rest for a fortnight". He still had the key; it hung by the door.

questions.stem: The rain is described as hitting the windows "like handfuls of gravel". What does this suggest about the rain?
options: It was heavy and hit the glass hard.
It was full of small stones.
It had only just started to fall.
questions.explanation: Gravel thrown at glass makes a hard, rattling noise, so the simile shows the rain was heavy and noisy. It does not mean real stones were falling.

questions.stem: Why did Mara take the key after she heard the ship's horn?
options: She realised a ship needed the light to stay safe.
She wanted to wake her grandfather up.
She was frightened of the storm and wanted to hide.
She had been told to light the lamp at that time.
questions.explanation: The horn tells her a ship is out in the storm, and a lighthouse warns ships away from rocks. Nobody had told her to go; she decided for herself.

questions.stem: In the sentence "slowly, solemnly, the beam began to sweep across the water", the word **solemnly** is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Solemnly means in a serious, dignified way, which suits the important moment of the light turning. Cheerfully and carelessly do not fit the careful mood.

questions.stem: How many stairs are there in the lighthouse?
questions.explanation: Mara counts the stairs "the way Grandad did: one hundred and twelve". The "hundred times" earlier is how often she had climbed them.

questions.stem: What does Grandad's nod at the end of the story show?
options: He was too tired to speak to her.
He was proud of Mara's careful work.
He was angry but did not want to shout.
He was surprised that the lamp still worked.
questions.explanation: The narrator says he nodded "the way he nodded at the end of a job well done", and he "did not scold her". That shows approval and pride, not anger.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of this text?
options: To explain hedgehogs' decline and how to help
To describe what hedgehogs look like
To persuade people to keep hedgehogs as pets
To tell a story about one hedgehog's journey
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives reasons numbers have fallen and the rest of the text lists ways to help. It never suggests keeping hedgehogs as pets.

questions.stem: According to the text, why do solid fences cause a problem for hedgehogs?
options: Hedgehogs injure themselves trying to climb them.
They make gardens too dark for hedgehogs to see.
They keep pets in gardens where hedgehogs live.
They stop hedgehogs reaching food and mates.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that if every garden is sealed off, a hedgehog "cannot reach enough food or find a mate".

questions.stem: How big should a hole in a fence be, according to the text?
options: Big enough for a cat to fit through
questions.explanation: The text says "about 13 centimetres square", which is big enough for a hedgehog "but too small for most pets".

questions.stem: The text says gardens are "sealed off". What does **sealed off** mean here?
questions.explanation: Sealed off means completely closed off. The writer is describing gardens surrounded by solid fences and walls.

questions.stem: Which of these does the text say you should NOT give to hedgehogs?
questions.explanation: The text warns "never put out bread or milk: milk can make hedgehogs very ill". Water and meaty pet food are suggested as safe.

questions.stem: Why does the writer call a chain of gardens a "hedgehog highway"?
options: Because hedgehogs are often hit by cars on highways
Because the holes are cut beside main roads
Because hedgehogs travel very fast through it
Because it gives them a long route, like a road
questions.explanation: A highway is a long main road. Linked gardens give hedgehogs a long safe route for their night-time journeys. The holes are in garden fences, not by roads.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**The children were / very excited about / the trip to the / musuem on Friday.**
questions.explanation: Museum is spelt m-u-s-e-u-m. The other parts are spelt correctly.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**We definately need / to buy more bread / before the shop / closes tonight.**
questions.explanation: Definitely is spelt d-e-f-i-n-i-t-e-l-y. It comes from finite, which helps you remember the i.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**My neighbour's cat / often sleeps / on our warm / kitchen windowsill.**
questions.explanation: Every word is spelt correctly. Neighbour is the British spelling, with -our.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**The scientist made / an amazing discovery / that suprised / everyone in the room.**
questions.explanation: Surprised has an r after the u: s-u-r-p-r-i-s-e-d.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**Have you seen / my blue jumper. / I can't find / it anywhere.**
questions.explanation: "Have you seen my blue jumper" is a question, so it needs a question mark, not a full stop.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**At the market / we bought apples pears, / plums and grapes / for our picnic.**
questions.explanation: Items in a list are separated by commas, so there should be a comma after apples: apples, pears, plums and grapes.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**The dogs bowl / was empty, so / I filled it / with fresh water.**
questions.explanation: The bowl belongs to the dog, so it needs an apostrophe: the dog's bowl.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**On Saturday, / we visited / Aunt Jo in / Manchester.**
questions.explanation: The comma after the fronted adverbial "On Saturday" is correct, and names have capital letters. There is no mistake.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Yesterday, we ___ to the beach.
questions.explanation: Yesterday tells us the sentence is in the past, so the simple past went is correct. Gone needs a helper such as have.

questions.stem:
Which word is a **verb** in this sentence?

The tired fox crept slowly through the hedge.
questions.explanation: A verb is a doing word. Crept is what the fox did. Tired is an adjective and slowly is an adverb.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The twins finished ___ homework before tea.
questions.explanation: Their shows that something belongs to them. There means a place and they're means they are.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

I could ___ gone with them if I had asked.
questions.explanation: Could have is correct. People sometimes write could of because could've sounds like it, but of is never right here.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Neither Sam nor his brothers ___ been to Scotland.
questions.explanation: With neither... nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Brothers is plural, so have is correct.
Add column by column: 8 + 9 = 17 (write 7, carry 1), 6 + 5 + 1 = 12 (write 2, carry 1), 3 + 7 + 1 = 11 (write 1, carry 1), 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. The answer is 7,127.

questions.stem: Pencils cost 35p each. How much do 8 pencils cost?
What is 46 × 7?
A rectangle is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: Perimeter is the distance all the way round: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 cm. 36 would be the area in cm².

questions.stem: What is the value of the digit 7 in 3.472?
questions.explanation: After the decimal point the places are tenths, hundredths, thousandths. In 3.472 the 4 is tenths, the 7 is hundredths and the 2 is thousandths.

questions.stem: A rectangular garden is 7 m long and 6 m wide. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area of a rectangle = length × width = 7 × 6 = 42 m².

questions.stem: What is $\frac{4}{7}$ of 63?
questions.explanation: Divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top: 63 ÷ 7 = 9, and 9 × 4 = 36. 9 is only one seventh.

questions.stem: How many grams are there in 2.5 kg?
What is 25% of 360?
questions.explanation: 25% is one quarter. 360 ÷ 4 = 90. 36 would be 10%.

questions.stem: What is 6,749 rounded to the nearest hundred?
questions.explanation: The hundreds digit is 7 and the next digit is 4. 4 is less than 5, so round down to 6,700.

questions.stem: A train leaves at 09:47. The journey takes 1 hour 25 minutes. What time does it arrive?
questions.explanation: 09:47 + 1 hour = 10:47. Then 13 more minutes reaches 11:00, and 12 more makes 25 minutes: 11:12.

questions.stem: Two angles in a triangle are 38° and 79°. What is the third angle?
questions.explanation: Angles in a triangle add up to 180°. 38 + 79 = 117, and 180 − 117 = 63°.

questions.stem: What is 936 ÷ 4?
questions.explanation: Short division: 9 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 1; 13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1; 16 ÷ 4 = 4. So 936 ÷ 4 = 234. Check: 234 × 4 = 936.

questions.stem: What is the mean of 4, 7, 9, 12 and 8?
questions.explanation: Add them: 4 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 8 = 40. Divide by how many there are: 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is the largest?
questions.explanation: Write them all with three decimal places: 0.610, 0.600, 0.590, 0.065, 0.609. The largest is 0.610, which is 0.61.

questions.stem: If 3n + 5 = 26, what is n?
questions.explanation: Take 5 from both sides: 3n = 21. Divide by 3: n = 7. Check: 3 × 7 + 5 = 26.

questions.stem: What is 3 + 4 × 5 − 2?
questions.explanation: Multiply before adding and subtracting: 4 × 5 = 20, then 3 + 20 − 2 = 21. Working left to right gives 33, which is wrong.

questions.stem:
Class 6 voted for their favourite pet.

| Pet | Votes |
|---|---|
| Dog | 12 |
| Cat | 8 |
| Rabbit | 5 |
| Fish | 3 |

How many more votes did Dog get than Rabbit and Fish together?
questions.explanation: Rabbit and Fish together: 5 + 3 = 8. Dog has 12. 12 − 8 = 4.

questions.stem: Which of these is a prime number?
questions.explanation: 47 has only two factors, 1 and 47. The others divide by 3: 39 = 3 × 13, 51 = 3 × 17, 57 = 3 × 19, 87 = 3 × 29.

questions.stem: A cuboid measures 7 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume = length × width × height = 7 × 4 × 3 = 84 cm³. 14 adds the lengths and 122 is the surface area.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{4}$?
questions.explanation: Use a common denominator of 12: $\frac{2}{3} = \frac{8}{12}$ and $\frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{12}$. 8 + 3 = 11, so the answer is $\frac{11}{12}$. Adding tops and bottoms (3/7) is wrong.

questions.stem: Notebooks are sold at 3 for £2. How much do 12 notebooks cost?
questions.explanation: 12 notebooks is 4 lots of 3. 4 × £2 = £8.

questions.stem: At 6 am the temperature was −7°C. By noon it had risen by 12 degrees. What was the temperature at noon?
questions.explanation: Count up from −7: 7 degrees takes you to 0, and 5 more takes you to 5°C.

questions.stem: The point (2, 6) is reflected in the x-axis. What are the coordinates of its new position?
questions.explanation: Reflecting in the x-axis keeps the x-coordinate the same and changes the sign of the y-coordinate: (2, 6) becomes (2, −6).

questions.stem: What is 0.4 × 0.3?
questions.explanation: 4 × 3 = 12. Each number has one decimal place, so the answer has two: 0.12.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to **brave**?
questions.explanation: Brave and courageous both mean ready to face danger or fear. Frightened is close to the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to **rapid**?
questions.explanation: Rapid means very fast, so quick is closest. Steady describes an even pace, not a fast one.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to **conceal**?
questions.explanation: To conceal something is to hide it. Reveal is the opposite, and seal only sounds similar.

questions.stem:
Find the letters that complete the series.

**BY, DX, FW, HV, ?**
questions.explanation: The first letters go B, D, F, H, J (forward 2 each time). The second letters go Y, X, W, V, U (back 1 each time). So the missing pair is JU.

questions.stem:
Find the letters that complete the series.

**CD, FE, ?, LG, OH**
questions.explanation: The first letters go C, F, I, L, O (forward 3 each time). The second letters go D, E, F, G, H (forward 1 each time). So the missing pair is IF.

questions.stem:
Find the letters that complete the series.

**AM, BO, DQ, GS, ?**
questions.explanation: The first letters go A, B, D, G, K (moving +1, then +2, then +3, then +4). The second letters go M, O, Q, S, U (forward 2 each time). So the missing pair is KU.

questions.stem: Which word is most opposite in meaning to **arrive**?
questions.explanation: To arrive is to get somewhere; to depart is to leave. Reach and enter mean nearly the same as arrive.

questions.stem: Which word is most opposite in meaning to **fragile**?
questions.explanation: Fragile means easily broken; sturdy means strong and hard to break. Delicate means nearly the same as fragile.

questions.stem: Which word is most opposite in meaning to **scarce**?
questions.explanation: Scarce means in short supply, so plentiful (more than enough) is the opposite. Uncommon means nearly the same as scarce.

questions.stem:
Find the pair that completes the sentence in the same way.

**BD** is to **CF** as **MP** is to **?**
questions.explanation: From BD to CF, B moves forward 1 to C and D moves forward 2 to F. Do the same to MP: M to N and P to R, giving NR.

questions.stem:
Find the pair that completes the sentence in the same way.

**GT** is to **EV** as **LK** is to **?**
questions.explanation: From GT to EV, G moves back 2 to E and T moves forward 2 to V. Do the same to LK: L to J and K to M, giving JM.

questions.stem:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which word is it?

**The old owl ate a mouse.**
questions.explanation: Read the words together: "owl ate" runs into LATE. None of the other words appear anywhere in the sentence.

questions.stem:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which word is it?

**The robot always beeps at noon.**
questions.explanation: Read the words together: "The robot" runs into HERO. None of the other words appear anywhere in the sentence.

questions.stem:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which word is it?

**She found the cave rather dark.**
questions.explanation: Read the words together: "rather dark" runs into HERD. None of the other words appear anywhere in the sentence.

questions.stem: If the code for **CAKE** is **DBLF**, what is the code for **MILK**?
questions.explanation: Each letter of CAKE moves forward 1 in the alphabet to make DBLF (C to D, A to B). Moving each letter of MILK forward 1 gives NJML.

questions.stem: If the code for **FROG** is **DPME**, what is the code for **SHIP**?
questions.explanation: Each letter of FROG moves back 2 in the alphabet to make DPME (F to D, R to P). Moving each letter of SHIP back 2 gives QFGN.

questions.stem: If **MAP** is written in code as **NBQ**, what does **DPX** mean?
questions.explanation: MAP becomes NBQ by moving each letter forward 1. To decode, move each letter of DPX back 1: D, P, X become C, O, W, which spells COW.

questions.stem:
Move one letter from the first word into the second word to make two new words. Which letter moves?

**BLEND   PAN**
questions.explanation: Take L out of BLEND to leave BEND, and put it into PAN to make PLAN. No other letter makes two real words.

questions.stem:
Move one letter from the first word into the second word to make two new words. Which letter moves?

**BRAKE   COW**
questions.explanation: Take R out of BRAKE to leave BAKE, and put it into COW to make CROW. No other letter makes two real words.

questions.stem: If **CART** is written as **2 4 7 1** and **TRAM** is written as **1 7 4 5**, what is the code for **MART**?
questions.explanation: Match each letter to its number: M = 5, A = 4, R = 7, T = 1. So MART is 5 4 7 1.

questions.stem: If **STOP** is written as **6 3 8 2**, which word is written as **3 8 2 6**?
questions.explanation: Turn each number back into its letter: 3 = T, 8 = O, 2 = P, 6 = S. The word is TOPS.

questions.stem: If **LINES** is written as **4 7 1 3 9**, what is the code for **LENS**?
questions.explanation: Match each letter to its number: L = 4, E = 3, N = 1, S = 9. So LENS is 4 3 1 9.

questions.stem:
Choose one word from each group that together make one new word. The word from the first group comes first.

**(car, bus, van)   (pet, ten, ear)**
questions.explanation: Car and pet make carpet. None of the other pairs make a real word.

questions.stem:
Choose one word from each group that together make one new word. The word from the first group comes first.

**(fire, ice, sea)   (cup, berg, rod)**
questions.explanation: Ice and berg make iceberg. None of the other pairs make a real word.

questions.stem:
Choose one word from each group that together make one new word. The word from the first group comes first.

**(star, moon, sun)   (ling, kit, pan)**
questions.explanation: Star and ling make starling. None of the other pairs make a real word.

questions.stem:
Find the number that comes next in the series.

**4, 9, 14, 19, ?**
questions.explanation: The numbers go up by 5 each time: 19 + 5 = 24.

questions.stem:
Find the number that comes next in the series.

**2, 5, 4, 7, 6, ?**
questions.explanation: The steps go up 3, down 1, up 3, down 1. The next step is up 3: 6 + 3 = 9.

questions.stem:
Find the number that comes next in the series.

**1, 2, 4, 7, 11, ?**
questions.explanation: The gap grows by 1 each time: +1, +2, +3, +4, so the next gap is +5. 11 + 5 = 16.

questions.stem:
The word in capitals has three letters missing. The missing letters make a three-letter word. Which is it?

**The STUT finished her homework early.**
questions.explanation: Put DEN back to make STUDENT: "The STUDENT finished her homework early."

questions.stem:
The word in capitals has three letters missing. The missing letters make a three-letter word. Which is it?

**An ELEPH sprayed water with its trunk.**
questions.explanation: Put ANT back to make ELEPHANT: "An ELEPHANT sprayed water with its trunk."

questions.stem:
If **A = 2, B = 3, C = 5, D = 6, E = 10**, what is the answer to this sum, written as a letter?

**A × B = ?**
questions.explanation: Swap each letter for its number: 2 × 3 = 6. The letter worth 6 is D.

questions.stem:
If **A = 4, B = 6, C = 8, D = 12, E = 24**, what is the answer to this sum, written as a letter?

**C × B ÷ A = ?**
questions.explanation: Swap each letter for its number: 8 × 6 ÷ 4 = 12. The letter worth 12 is D.

questions.stem:
Three of these words go together. Which two do not belong with them?

**apple, pear, carrot, plum, cabbage**
questions.explanation: Apple, pear and plum are fruits. Carrot and cabbage are vegetables.

questions.stem:
Three of these words go together. Which two do not belong with them?

**whisper, shout, mutter, yell, murmur**
questions.explanation: Whisper, mutter and murmur are all ways of speaking quietly. Shout and yell are loud.

questions.stem:
The number in brackets is made from the two outside numbers in the same way in each group. Find the missing number.

**(4 [20] 5)   (3 [18] 6)   (7 [?] 3)**
questions.explanation: In each group the outside numbers are multiplied: 4 × 5 = 20, 3 × 6 = 18. So 7 × 3 = 21.

questions.stem:
The number in brackets is made from the two outside numbers in the same way in each group. Find the missing number.

**(2 [10] 3)   (4 [14] 3)   (5 [?] 6)**
questions.explanation: Add the outside numbers and double: (2 + 3) × 2 = 10, (4 + 3) × 2 = 14. So (5 + 6) × 2 = 22.

questions.stem:
Which word completes the sentence in the best way?

**Puppy** is to **dog** as **kitten** is to **?**
questions.explanation: A puppy is a young dog, so a kitten is a young cat.

questions.stem:
Which word completes the sentence in the best way?

**Author** is to **book** as **composer** is to **?**
questions.explanation: An author writes a book; a composer writes music. A concert is where music is played, not what a composer writes.

questions.stem:
Amir is taller than Ben. Chloe is shorter than Ben. Dev is taller than Amir.

Who is the shortest?
questions.explanation: Put them in order from tallest: Dev, Amir, Ben, Chloe. Chloe is shorter than Ben, and Ben is shorter than both Amir and Dev.

questions.stem:
Ella, Finn, Gus and Hana each walk the dog on one day, Monday to Thursday, all on different days. Hana walks on Monday. Gus walks the day after Hana. Finn walks the day after Ella.

On which day does Finn walk?
questions.explanation: Hana is Monday, so Gus is Tuesday. Wednesday and Thursday are left, and Finn must come the day after Ella: Ella Wednesday, Finn Thursday.

questions.stem: How did Sami protect the pumpkin from rotting?
options: He covered it with a sheet.
He moved it into the shed.
questions.explanation: The passage says he "laid straw under the swelling fruit so it would not rot on the damp ground". Watering was for when the soil was dry, not to stop rot.

questions.stem: Why does Sami think "This is our year" is something he "had heard before"?
options: Grandad had already won the contest once.
Grandad says it every year but always comes second.
Mrs Okafor had told him the same thing.
Sami had read it on the seed packet.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says Grandad enters every year and always comes second, so his hopeful words are familiar. Nothing says he had ever won.

questions.stem: The pumpkin's skin is described as "glowing orange like a sunset". This simile mainly suggests that the pumpkin:
options: was growing more slowly in the evening
questions.explanation: A sunset is a warm, glowing orange, so the comparison describes the pumpkin's bright colour. It says nothing about weight or rotting.

questions.stem: How was Grandad most likely feeling on the walk home?
questions.explanation: He had hoped this was his year, then lost by just two kilograms, and he "was quiet on the walk home". That suggests disappointment.

questions.stem: "Mrs Okafor, whose pumpkins were **rumoured** to be fed on a secret mixture". Rumoured means:
options: proven to be true by the judges
written about in the local newspaper
said by people but not known to be true
kept secret in a locked shed
questions.explanation: A rumour is something people say that has not been checked. At the end, Mrs Okafor reveals the rumour was false.

questions.stem: Which sentence best sums up the message of the story?
options: Winning is the only thing that counts.
You should never trust your neighbours.
Big vegetables need special food to grow.
questions.explanation: Mrs Okafor says there is "no secret mixture... just patience", and she praises Sami's daily care. The story ends by showing that simple, steady work is what counts.

questions.stem: According to the text, when was the last frost fair held?
questions.explanation: The final paragraph begins: "The last frost fair was held in 1814."

questions.stem: How did the old London Bridge help the river to freeze?
options: It blocked the warm sea air.
It stopped boats from breaking up the ice.
Its stone supports were very cold.
Its narrow arches slowed the water down.
questions.explanation: The text says the narrow arches "slowed the river down above the bridge", and slow water freezes more easily than fast water.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the word **milder** most nearly means:
questions.explanation: Mild weather is gentle and not extreme. Milder winters are less cold, which is why the river no longer freezes.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT mentioned as something you could find at a frost fair?
questions.explanation: The text lists hot food, gingerbread, drinks, skittles, puppet shows and printing presses. Skating races are never mentioned.

questions.stem: Why might visitors have wanted a card "printed on the Thames"?
options: As a souvenir of their day at the fair
Because paper was cheaper on the ice
So they could find their way home
Because it was a ticket to enter the fair
questions.explanation: A card with your own name, printed on the frozen river itself, is a keepsake of an unusual day. Nothing suggests it was a ticket or a map.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the final paragraph?
options: To describe the games played at the fairs
To warn readers about thin ice
To describe the old London Bridge
To explain why frost fairs no longer happen
questions.explanation: The last paragraph lists the changes (a new bridge, embankments, milder winters) that mean the river is unlikely to freeze again.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**Mrs Patel asked us / to write a peice / of poetry about / the autumn leaves.**
questions.explanation: Piece is spelt p-i-e-c-e: "a piece of pie" helps you remember the i comes first.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**It was a / beautiful morning / so we walked / accross the fields.**
questions.explanation: Across has only one c: a-c-r-o-s-s.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**The library is / closed on Sundays / and on every / bank holiday.**
questions.explanation: Every word is spelt correctly, so there is no mistake.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**Our football team / recieved a trophy / at the end / of the season.**
questions.explanation: Received follows "i before e except after c": r-e-c-e-i-v-e-d.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**"Hurry up," / shouted Dad / "or we'll miss / the train!"**
questions.explanation: When speech is split by "shouted Dad", a comma is needed before the speech starts again: "Hurry up," shouted Dad, "or we'll miss the train!"

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**Its going to / rain later, / so take your / umbrella with you.**
questions.explanation: It's is short for it is, so it needs an apostrophe: It's going to rain.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**My sister, / who loves horses, / goes riding / every weekend.**
questions.explanation: The commas correctly mark off the extra information "who loves horses". There is no mistake.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**i asked my / teacher if we / could go outside / at lunchtime.**
questions.explanation: The word I is always a capital letter, and a sentence must start with one too.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

There were ___ people at the match than last week.
questions.explanation: People can be counted, so fewer is correct. Less is used for things that cannot be counted, such as less water.

questions.stem:
Which word is an **adjective** in this sentence?

The curious cat watched the bird.
questions.explanation: An adjective describes a noun. Curious describes the cat. Watched is a verb and cat and bird are nouns.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Mia and ___ are going to the park.
questions.explanation: Take Mia away and test it: "I am going to the park" is right, but "me am going" is not. So it is Mia and I.

questions.stem:
Which word is a **preposition** in this sentence?

We hid underneath the stairs.
questions.explanation: A preposition shows where something is in relation to something else. Underneath tells us where we hid.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence in formal standard English.

If I ___ you, I would take a coat.
questions.explanation: This is the subjunctive, used for something imagined: if I were you. Was is common in speech but were is the formal standard form.

questions.stem: What is 802 − 367?
Two angles sit together on a straight line. One is 137°. What is the other?
questions.explanation: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. 180 − 137 = 43°.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{7}{8}$ of 64?
How many metres are there in 3.2 km?
Which of these is a square number between 50 and 70?
questions.explanation: 8 × 8 = 64, which is between 50 and 70. 49 (7 × 7) is a square number but is less than 50.

questions.stem: How many edges does a cube have?
questions.explanation: A cube has 4 edges round the top, 4 round the bottom and 4 going up the sides: 12. It has 6 faces and 8 vertices.

questions.stem: What is 4.6 × 100?
questions.explanation: Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left: 4.6 becomes 460.

questions.stem: Cinema tickets cost £4.75 each. Mo buys 3 tickets and pays with a £20 note. How much change does he get?
What is 58 × 24?
A triangle has a base of 12 cm and a perpendicular height of 7 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area of a triangle = half × base × height = ½ × 12 × 7 = 42 cm². 84 forgets to halve.

questions.stem: What is 1,500 ÷ 12?
A film starts at 18:40 and lasts 135 minutes. At what time does it finish?
questions.explanation: 135 minutes = 2 hours 15 minutes. 18:40 + 2 hours = 20:40, then + 15 minutes = 20:55.

questions.stem: What is 15% of 80?
questions.explanation: 10% of 80 is 8 and 5% is half of that, 4. 8 + 4 = 12.

questions.stem: The rule for a sequence is: multiply the position number by 4, then subtract 1. What is the 10th number in the sequence?

questions.explanation: Brackets first: 6 + 9 = 15. Then divide and multiply from left to right: 15 ÷ 3 = 5, and 5 × 2 = 10.

questions.stem: A pie chart shows the favourite sports of 24 children. The football sector has an angle of 90°. How many children chose football?
questions.explanation: 90° is a quarter of the full 360°. A quarter of 24 children is 6.

questions.stem: What is 0.35 as a fraction in its simplest form?
questions.explanation: 0.35 is 35 hundredths, $\frac{35}{100}$. Divide top and bottom by 5 to get $\frac{7}{20}$.

questions.stem: A recipe for 6 people uses 360 g of flour. How much flour is needed for 15 people?
questions.explanation: For 1 person: 360 ÷ 6 = 60 g. For 15 people: 60 × 15 = 900 g.

questions.stem: What is the lowest common multiple of 6 and 8?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24... and 24 is the first one that 6 also divides. 48 is a common multiple but not the lowest; 2 is a common factor.

questions.stem: A car travels at 60 km per hour. How far does it travel in 2 hours 30 minutes?
questions.explanation: In 2 hours it goes 120 km, and in half an hour 30 km more. 120 + 30 = 150 km. 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.5 hours, not 2.3.

questions.stem: £40 is shared between Asha and Ben in the ratio 3 : 5. How much does Ben get?
questions.explanation: 3 + 5 = 8 parts. £40 ÷ 8 = £5 a part. Ben has 5 parts: 5 × £5 = £25. Asha gets £15.

questions.stem: Which of these shapes has exactly 2 lines of symmetry?
questions.explanation: A non-square rectangle folds in half two ways: across the middle and down the middle. A square has 4, an equilateral triangle 3, a regular hexagon 6 and a kite 1.

questions.stem: What is 1.2 − 0.35?
The mean of five numbers is 6. Four of the numbers are 3, 5, 8 and 9. What is the fifth number?
questions.explanation: If the mean of five numbers is 6, their total is 5 × 6 = 30. 3 + 5 + 8 + 9 = 25. The fifth number is 30 − 25 = 5.

questions.stem: Which of these fractions is the smallest?
questions.explanation: Compare each with one half: every fraction here is a little more than a half. 4/7 is 1/14 more than a half, 7/12 is 1/12 more, 3/5 is 1/10 more, 5/8 is 1/8 more and 2/3 is 1/6 more. 1/14 is the smallest extra, so 4/7 is smallest.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to **furious**?
questions.explanation: Furious means extremely angry. Curious only sounds similar; it means wanting to know.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to **ancient**?
questions.explanation: Ancient means very old, like ancient ruins. Broken, famous and precious things can be new.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to **timid**?
questions.explanation: A timid person is easily frightened and lacks confidence, which is close to shy. Tiny only sounds similar.

questions.stem:
Find the letters that complete the series.

**DK, FL, HM, JN, ?**
questions.explanation: The first letters go D, F, H, J, L (forward 2 each time). The second letters go K, L, M, N, O (forward 1 each time). So the missing pair is LO.

questions.stem:
Find the letters that complete the series.

**QB, ?, MH, KK, IN**
questions.explanation: The first letters go Q, O, M, K, I (back 2 each time). The second letters go B, E, H, K, N (forward 3 each time). So the missing pair is OE.

questions.stem:
Find the letters that complete the series.

**CW, DV, FT, IQ, ?**
questions.explanation: The first letters go C, D, F, I, M (moving +1, then +2, then +3, then +4). The second letters go W, V, T, Q, M (moving -1, then -2, then -3, then -4). So the missing pair is MM.

questions.stem: Which word is most opposite in meaning to **generous**?
questions.explanation: A generous person gives freely; a selfish person keeps things for themselves. Kind is close to generous, not opposite.

questions.stem: Which word is most opposite in meaning to **expand**?
questions.explanation: To expand is to get bigger; to shrink is to get smaller. Stretch and grow are close to expand.

questions.stem: Which word is most opposite in meaning to **victory**?
questions.explanation: A victory is a win and a defeat is a loss. Triumph means nearly the same as victory.

questions.stem:
Find the pair that completes the sentence in the same way.

**AZ** is to **BY** as **HS** is to **?**
questions.explanation: From AZ to BY, A moves forward 1 to B and Z moves back 1 to Y. Do the same to HS: H to I and S to R, giving IR.

questions.stem:
Find the pair that completes the sentence in the same way.

**PR** is to **SU** as **DF** is to **?**
questions.explanation: From PR to SU, P moves forward 3 to S and R moves forward 3 to U. Do the same to DF: D to G and F to I, giving GI.

questions.stem:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which word is it?

**The zebra in the zoo was asleep.**
questions.explanation: Read the words together: "zebra in" runs into RAIN. None of the other words appear anywhere in the sentence.

questions.stem:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which word is it?

**Tim's cousin kept a pet frog.**
questions.explanation: Read the words together: "cousin kept" runs into SINK. None of the other words appear anywhere in the sentence.

questions.stem:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which word is it?

**Please ask Mum for the scissors.**
questions.explanation: Read the words together: "for the" runs into FORT. None of the other words appear anywhere in the sentence.

questions.stem: If the code for **LAMP** is **NCOR**, what is the code for **DESK**?
questions.explanation: Each letter of LAMP moves forward 2 in the alphabet to make NCOR (L to N, A to C). Moving each letter of DESK forward 2 gives FGUM.

questions.stem: If **BED** is written in code as **EHG**, what does **GRJ** mean?
questions.explanation: BED becomes EHG by moving each letter forward 3. To decode, move each letter of GRJ back 3: G, R, J become D, O, G, which spells DOG.

questions.stem: In a code, **GOAL** is written as **TLZO**. What is **FISH** in the same code?
questions.explanation: Each letter is swapped for its mirror in the alphabet: A and Z, B and Y, C and X, and so on (the two positions add to 27). GOAL becomes TLZO, so FISH becomes URHS.

questions.stem:
Move one letter from the first word into the second word to make two new words. Which letter moves?

**CLAMP   BAD**
questions.explanation: Take L out of CLAMP to leave CAMP, and put it into BAD to make BALD. No other letter makes two real words.

questions.stem:
Move one letter from the first word into the second word to make two new words. Which letter moves?

**CRANE   BOW**
questions.explanation: Take R out of CRANE to leave CANE, and put it into BOW to make BROW. No other letter makes two real words.

questions.stem: If **BOATS** is written as **5 2 8 6 3**, what is the code for **STAB**?
questions.explanation: Match each letter to its number: S = 3, T = 6, A = 8, B = 5. So STAB is 3 6 8 5.

questions.stem: If **MEAT** is written as **4 7 2 9** and **TEAM** is written as **9 7 2 4**, which word is written as **2 9 7**?
questions.explanation: Turn each number back into its letter: 2 = A, 9 = T, 7 = E. The word is ATE.

questions.stem: If **SNOW** is written as **6 1 4 8** and **WON** is written as **8 4 1**, which word is written as **1 4 8**?
questions.explanation: Turn each number back into its letter: 1 = N, 4 = O, 8 = W. The word is NOW.

questions.stem:
Choose one word from each group that together make one new word. The word from the first group comes first.

**(hand, foot, arm)   (bag, cot, pin)**
questions.explanation: Hand and bag make handbag. None of the other pairs make a real word.

questions.stem:
Choose one word from each group that together make one new word. The word from the first group comes first.

**(rain, wind, snow)   (bow, toe, lid)**
questions.explanation: Rain and bow make rainbow. None of the other pairs make a real word.

questions.stem:
Choose one word from each group that together make one new word. The word from the first group comes first.

**(pass, tree, milk)   (word, lamp, mat)**
questions.explanation: Pass and word make password. None of the other pairs make a real word.

questions.stem:
Find the number that comes next in the series.

**81, 72, 63, 54, ?**
questions.explanation: The numbers go down by 9 each time: 54 - 9 = 45.

questions.stem:
Find the number that comes next in the series.

**1, 4, 9, 16, ?**
questions.explanation: These are the square numbers: 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, 4 × 4. Next is 5 × 5 = 25. (The gaps +3, +5, +7 lead to +9 as well.)

questions.stem:
Find the number that comes next in the series.

**2, 20, 4, 18, 6, 16, ?**
questions.explanation: Two series take turns. One goes 2, 4, 6 (up 2) and the other goes 20, 18, 16 (down 2). The next number belongs to the first series: 6 + 2 = 8.

questions.stem:
The word in capitals has three letters missing. The missing letters make a three-letter word. Which is it?

**The MON grabbed a banana.**
questions.explanation: Put KEY back to make MONKEY: "The MONKEY grabbed a banana."

questions.stem:
The word in capitals has three letters missing. The missing letters make a three-letter word. Which is it?

**The SOLRS marched past the palace.**
questions.explanation: Put DIE back to make SOLDIERS: "The SOLDIERS marched past the palace."

questions.stem:
If **A = 3, B = 5, C = 8, D = 15, E = 24**, what is the answer to this sum, written as a letter?

**A × B = ?**
questions.explanation: Swap each letter for its number: 3 × 5 = 15. The letter worth 15 is D.

questions.stem:
If **A = 2, B = 4, C = 7, D = 10, E = 14**, what is the answer to this sum, written as a letter?

**(D + B) ÷ A = ?**
questions.explanation: Swap each letter for its number: (10 + 4) ÷ 2 = 7. The letter worth 7 is C.

questions.stem:
Three of these words go together. Which two do not belong with them?

**robin, salmon, sparrow, trout, eagle**
questions.explanation: Robin, sparrow and eagle are birds. Salmon and trout are fish.

questions.stem:
Three of these words go together. Which two do not belong with them?

**circle, cube, square, sphere, triangle**
questions.explanation: Circle, square and triangle are flat (2-D) shapes. A cube and a sphere are solid (3-D) shapes.

questions.stem:
The number in brackets is made from the two outside numbers in the same way in each group. Find the missing number.

**(24 [6] 4)   (35 [5] 7)   (54 [?] 9)**
questions.explanation: The first number is divided by the second: 24 ÷ 4 = 6, 35 ÷ 7 = 5. So 54 ÷ 9 = 6.

questions.stem:
The number in brackets is made from the two outside numbers in the same way in each group. Find the missing number.

**(3 [13] 4)   (5 [11] 2)   (6 [?] 4)**
questions.explanation: Multiply the outside numbers and add 1: 3 × 4 + 1 = 13, 5 × 2 + 1 = 11. So 6 × 4 + 1 = 25.

questions.stem:
Which word completes the sentence in the best way?

**Hot** is to **cold** as **wet** is to **?**
questions.explanation: Hot and cold are opposites, so the pair for wet is its opposite, dry. Damp means nearly the same as wet.

questions.stem:
Which word completes the sentence in the best way?

**Hand** is to **glove** as **foot** is to **?**
questions.explanation: A glove is worn on the hand and a sock is worn on the foot. Toe, ankle and heel are parts of the foot.

questions.stem: If the day after tomorrow is Saturday, what day was yesterday?
questions.explanation: The day after tomorrow is Saturday, so tomorrow is Friday and today is Thursday. Yesterday was Wednesday.

questions.stem:
Every member of the chess club is in Year 6. Some Year 6 pupils play football. Lily is in the chess club.

Which of these must be true?
options: Every Year 6 pupil is in the chess club.
Some chess club members play football.
questions.explanation: Lily is in the chess club and every member is in Year 6, so she must be in Year 6. Nothing says whether any chess player, Lily included, plays football.

questions.stem: The train is called "a lantern-snake of gold". Which feature of the train does this image describe?
options: The loud noise of the engine
A snake that lives beside the railway
A long line of lit windows in the dark
The gold paint on the carriages
questions.explanation: A snake is long and winding, and lanterns give light. Together they picture a long, glowing train curving through the night, not a real snake.

questions.stem: Which animals are mentioned in the second verse?
questions.explanation: The second verse says "The cows lie dreaming in the fields, / the owls look up and stare".

questions.stem: Why does the girl count "four more, three more, two more, one"?
options: She is counting stops until home.
She is counting the people in her carriage.
She is trying to fall asleep.
She is practising her times tables.
questions.explanation: The poem says she "counts stations on her hand", ending with "her own home land". She is counting down to her stop.

questions.stem: In the line "it **threads** the sleeping villages", the word threads suggests the train:
options: ties the villages together with a string
wakes everyone up as it passes
passes through, like a needle through cloth
questions.explanation: Threading a needle means passing it through small gaps. The verb pictures the train weaving through one village after another.

questions.stem: Which line gives the train a human action?
options: "The cows lie dreaming in the fields"
questions.explanation: Whispering is something people do, so it personifies the train. The other lines describe the cows, the grandma and the girl, who are not the train.

questions.stem: How does the mood change in the last verse?
questions.explanation: The cold, sleepy night ends with Grandma waiting and "warmth comes rushing in". The ending feels like a homecoming.

questions.stem: Why did Mary first start collecting fossils?
options: To help her poor family earn money
Because she was a member of a science society
Because her teacher asked her to
To build a museum in Lyme Regis
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says her family was poor and she collected fossils "selling them to visitors" to help earn money.

questions.stem: Which description matches a plesiosaur?
options: A sea reptile with a long, toothed snout
A fish with a hard shell
A bird that lived on the cliffs
A reptile with a very long neck
questions.explanation: The text describes a plesiosaur as having "a small head and a very long neck". The long, toothed snout belongs to the ichthyosaur.

questions.stem: Why were the best fossils found after storms?
options: Storms washed fossils in from the sea.
There were fewer visitors on the beach.
Fresh rock fell from the cliffs.
The rain made the fossils shine.
questions.explanation: The text says the best finds appeared after storms, "when fresh rock fell from the cliffs".

questions.stem: "Mary did not always receive the **credit** she deserved." Here, credit means:
options: money kept in a bank account
a prize at the village show
questions.explanation: Credit here means being recognised for something you did. The next sentence explains that men described her finds without naming her.

questions.stem: What does the fourth paragraph suggest about life for women scientists at that time?
options: They were paid more than men.
They were not interested in fossils.
questions.explanation: Mary could not join the Geological Society because she was a woman, and others took credit for her work. That shows unfair treatment.

questions.stem: Which would be the best alternative title for this text?
options: How to Find Fossils on the Beach
The Life of Tray the Dog
The Fossil Hunter Who Changed History
questions.explanation: The text is about Mary's life and how her discoveries helped people understand extinct animals. It is not a how-to guide or a history of Dorset.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**Dad said it was / necesary to wear / a helmet when / cycling to school.**
questions.explanation: Necessary has one c and two s: n-e-c-e-s-s-a-r-y. Think "one collar, two sleeves".

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**The weather forecast / promised sunshine, / but it rained / untill teatime.**
questions.explanation: Until has only one l at the end, although till has two.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a spelling mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**Grandma keeps / a seperate drawer / for birthday cards / and wrapping paper.**
questions.explanation: Separate is spelt s-e-p-a-r-a-t-e: there is "a rat" in separate.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**The childrens / coats were hanging / on the pegs / by the door.**
questions.explanation: The coats belong to the children, so it should be children's. Children is already plural, so the apostrophe goes before the s.

questions.stem:
Which part of this sentence contains a punctuation mistake? If there is no mistake, choose **No mistake**.

**The Eiffel Tower / is in paris, / the capital / of France.**
questions.explanation: Paris is the name of a city, so it needs a capital letter.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The cake was ___ big for one person to eat.
questions.explanation: Too means more than enough. To shows direction and two is the number 2.

questions.stem:
Which word is a **pronoun** in this sentence?

Ravi lent the book to them.
questions.explanation: A pronoun stands in place of a noun. Them replaces the names of the people Ravi lent the book to.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

She ran ___ than anyone else in the race.
questions.explanation: Than tells us two things are being compared, so the comparative faster is correct. Fastest is used with the, as in the fastest.

questions.stem: What is the plural of **knife**?
questions.explanation: Many words ending in -fe change to -ves in the plural: knife, knives; wife, wives. Plurals never need an apostrophe.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

I wanted to play outside, ___ it was pouring with rain.
questions.explanation: The two parts contrast: I wanted to go out, yet it was raining. But is the conjunction that shows a contrast.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{3}{4}$ of 120?
Sandwiches cost £3.45 each and a juice costs £1.20. How much do 2 sandwiches and a juice cost?
What is 20% of 45?
questions.explanation: 10% of 45 is 4.5, so 20% is double that: 9.

questions.stem: What is the value of 2a + 3 when a = 6?
questions.explanation: 2a means 2 × a. 2 × 6 = 12, and 12 + 3 = 15. 26 comes from writing 2 next to 6.

questions.stem: Which number is a factor of both 24 and 36?
questions.explanation: 24 = 12 × 2 and 36 = 12 × 3. 8 divides 24 but not 36; 9 and 18 divide 36 but not 24; 16 divides neither.

questions.stem: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 90°, 110° and 70°. What is the fourth angle?
questions.explanation: Angles in a quadrilateral add up to 360°. 90 + 110 + 70 = 270, and 360 − 270 = 90°.
Brackets first: 8 − 3 = 5. Then multiply: 5 × 5 = 25. Then add: 25 + 4 = 29.

questions.stem: What is 750 ml + 1.5 litres, in litres?
How many minutes are there between 10:45 and 13:20?
questions.explanation: 10:45 to 13:00 is 2 hours 15 minutes, which is 135 minutes. 13:00 to 13:20 is 20 more. 135 + 20 = 155 minutes.

questions.stem: Which decimal is equal to $\frac{3}{8}$?

Here are the midday temperatures for five days.

| Day | Temperature |
|---|---|
| Mon | 4°C |
| Tue | −2°C |
| Wed | 1°C |
| Thu | −5°C |
| Fri | 3°C |

What is the difference between the highest and lowest temperatures?
questions.explanation: The highest is 4°C (Monday) and the lowest is −5°C (Thursday). From −5 up to 0 is 5 degrees and 0 up to 4 is 4 more: 9 degrees.

questions.stem: What is 2 − 7 + 3?
questions.explanation: Work left to right: 2 − 7 = −5, then −5 + 3 = −2.

questions.stem: A ribbon 3 m long is cut into pieces 25 cm long. How many pieces are there?
What is 15.649 rounded to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: Look at the hundredths digit, 4. It is less than 5, so the tenths digit stays: 15.6. Do not round 15.649 to 15.65 first.

questions.stem: A, B, C and D are the corners of a rectangle. A is at (1, 1), B is at (5, 1) and C is at (5, 4). Where is D?
questions.explanation: D must be straight above A and level with C. It takes A's x-coordinate, 1, and C's y-coordinate, 4: (1, 4).

questions.stem: I think of a number, double it and add 7. The answer is 31. What was my number?
questions.explanation: Work backwards: 31 − 7 = 24, then halve: 24 ÷ 2 = 12. Check: 12 × 2 + 7 = 31.

questions.stem: $\frac{2}{5}$ of a number is 18. What is the number?
questions.explanation: If 2 fifths are 18, one fifth is 9. Five fifths are 5 × 9 = 45. Check: 45 ÷ 5 × 2 = 18.

questions.stem: 30% of the price of a coat is £12. What is the full price?
A square has an area of 36 cm². What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: The side length is 6 cm, because 6 × 6 = 36. Perimeter = 4 × 6 = 24 cm.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to **reluctant**?
questions.explanation: Reluctant means not wanting to do something, so unwilling is closest. Eager is the opposite.

questions.stem:
Find the letters that complete the series.

**HS, KQ, NO, ?, TK**
questions.explanation: The first letters go H, K, N, Q, T (forward 3 each time). The second letters go S, Q, O, M, K (back 2 each time). So the missing pair is QM.

questions.stem: Which word is most opposite in meaning to **temporary**?
questions.explanation: Temporary means lasting a short time; permanent means lasting for ever. Brief is close to temporary.

questions.stem:
Find the pair that completes the sentence in the same way.

**KM** is to **JO** as **TV** is to **?**
questions.explanation: From KM to JO, K moves back 1 to J and M moves forward 2 to O. Do the same to TV: T to S and V to X, giving SX.

questions.stem:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which word is it?

**The swan dived under the bridge.**
questions.explanation: Read the words together: "swan dived" runs into WAND. None of the other words appear anywhere in the sentence.

questions.stem: If the code for **PLAN** is **QMBO**, what is the code for **BIRD**?
questions.explanation: Each letter of PLAN moves forward 1 in the alphabet to make QMBO (P to Q, L to M). Moving each letter of BIRD forward 1 gives CJSE.

questions.stem:
Move one letter from the first word into the second word to make two new words. Which letter moves?

**PLANT   CAP**
questions.explanation: Take L out of PLANT to leave PANT, and put it into CAP to make CLAP. No other letter makes two real words.

questions.stem: If **PLANE** is written as **3 6 9 2 5**, what is the code for **PANEL**?
questions.explanation: Match each letter to its number: P = 3, A = 9, N = 2, E = 5, L = 6. So PANEL is 3 9 2 5 6.

questions.stem:
Choose one word from each group that together make one new word. The word from the first group comes first.

**(cup, plate, bowl)   (board, pen, tin)**
questions.explanation: Cup and board make cupboard. None of the other pairs make a real word.

questions.stem:
Find the number that comes next in the series.

**3, 6, 12, 24, ?**
questions.explanation: Each number is double the one before: 24 × 2 = 48.

questions.stem:
The word in capitals has three letters missing. The missing letters make a three-letter word. Which is it?

**My PNTS took us to the zoo.**
questions.explanation: Put ARE back to make PARENTS: "My PARENTS took us to the zoo."

questions.stem:
If **A = 5, B = 6, C = 11, D = 30, E = 36**, what is the answer to this sum, written as a letter?

**A × B + B = ?**
questions.explanation: Swap each letter for its number: 5 × 6 + 6 = 36. The letter worth 36 is E.

questions.stem:
Three of these words go together. Which two do not belong with them?

**gigantic, tiny, enormous, minute, huge**
questions.explanation: Gigantic, enormous and huge all mean very big. Tiny and minute (said my-NEWT) both mean very small.

questions.stem:
The number in brackets is made from the two outside numbers in the same way in each group. Find the missing number.

**(8 [3] 2)   (11 [4] 3)   (17 [?] 5)**
questions.explanation: Take the second number from the first, then halve: (8 - 2) ÷ 2 = 3, (11 - 3) ÷ 2 = 4. So (17 - 5) ÷ 2 = 6.

questions.stem:
Which word completes the sentence in the best way?

**Bee** is to **hive** as **bird** is to **?**
questions.explanation: A bee's home is a hive and a bird's home is a nest. A bird may nest in a tree, but the nest is the home it builds.

questions.stem:
Jo has more marbles than Kit but fewer than Lee. Mo has more marbles than Lee.

Who has the second most marbles?
questions.explanation: From most to fewest: Mo, Lee, Jo, Kit. Mo beats Lee, and Lee beats Jo, who beats Kit.
